intro: Educated German (Bildungssprache) draws on a stock of Latin-derived words and phrases that rarely occur in everyday talk but run through every quality newspaper, court judgment and academic text: evident, eruieren, obsolet, prekär, konzedieren, implizieren, subsumieren, stringent, sukzessive, and set Latin phrases such as a priori, de facto, per se, ad hoc, Status quo and sui generis. The goal is to read them without hesitation and use them precisely in your own writing. In this quiz the German line above each sentence gives a plain paraphrase and the cue gives the English; type the Fremdwort, inflected to fit the sentence (prekären, konzediert, eruiert). Adjectives and verbs follow normal German grammar; the Latin phrases never inflect. Watch out for false friends with English: eventuell means possibly, not eventually, and konsequent means consistent, not consequent.
tips[0].title: German grammar on Latin stems
tips[0].text: Verbs in -ieren are regular and take no ge- in the Partizip II: eruieren → eruiert, konzedieren → konzediert, implizieren → impliziert, subsumieren → subsumiert. Adjectives take normal endings: unter prekären Bedingungen, eine stringente Argumentation, ein obsoletes Verfahren. Nouns keep their gender: das Desiderat, die Prämisse, der Status quo, das Diktum.
tips[0].trap: geeruiert or gekonzediert do not exist: verbs in -ieren never take ge-.
tips[0].check.why: Verbs in -ieren never take ge- in the Partizip II: identifiziert, like eruiert and konzediert.
tips[1].title: Latin phrases stay invariable
tips[1].text: a priori (von vornherein), a posteriori (aus der Erfahrung, im Nachhinein), de facto (tatsächlich) vs de jure (rechtlich), per se (an sich), ad hoc (eigens, spontan), sui generis (eigener Art), Status quo (bestehender Zustand), ceteris paribus (unter sonst gleichen Bedingungen). They take no endings; only Status quo behaves like a noun with an article: den Status quo wahren.
tips[1].check.why: de jure means by law, as opposed to de facto, in actual practice.
tips[2].title: Precision, not decoration
tips[2].text: Each Fremdwort says something the everyday word does not quite say. evident is stronger than klar; stringent describes the logic of an argument, not its strictness; marginal means negligible in extent; ambivalent means torn between two feelings, not indifferent; kontraproduktiv means working against one’s own goal. Use one where it sharpens the statement — a sentence stuffed with Latinisms reads as pompous.
tips[2].trap: ambivalent is not indifferent (gleichgültig): an ambivalent person feels two things at once.
tips[2].check.why: ambivalent means torn between two feelings at once, not indifferent (gleichgültig).
tips[3].title: Beware of English look-alikes
tips[3].text: Several Latinate words mean something different in German. eventuell = possibly (eventually = schließlich); konsequent = consistent, rigorous (consequent = folgend); sensibel = sensitive (sensible = vernünftig); prägnant = concise (pregnant = schwanger); rentabel = profitable. Check every look-alike before you use it in an essay.
tips[3].check.why: German sensibel means sensitive; English 'sensible' is vernünftig, and prägnant means concise.

remember[0]: Verbs in -ieren: no ge- in the Partizip II (eruiert, konzediert, impliziert).
remember[1]: Adjectives inflect normally (unter prekären Bedingungen); Latin phrases never do (a priori, de facto, per se, ad hoc).
remember[2]: Use a Fremdwort for precision, not decoration — one per sentence is usually enough.
remember[3]: False friends: eventuell = possibly, konsequent = consistent, sensibel = sensitive.
mistakes[0].why: Verbs in -ieren form the Partizip II without ge-.
mistakes[1].why: eventuell means possibly; for eventually German uses schließlich or letztendlich.
mistakes[2].why: A Latin-derived adjective before a noun takes the normal German ending.
mistakes[3].why: ambivalent means torn between opposing feelings, not indifferent.
hook: Handle the Latin-flavoured words of serious German prose, like eruieren, obsolet and de facto, precisely and without false friends.
tips[1].check.q: 'Legally she owns the firm, but in practice her brother runs it.' ____ ist sie die Eigentümerin.
